witness_description: Triangle on vertices {0,1,2} with edges (0,1), (0,2), (1,2) all of weight 1. The only simple cycle is the triangle itself, whose maximum edge weight is 1, so ALL three edges are maximum-weight edges of a cycle. Every minimum spanning tree (there are three, each consisting of two edges of total weight 2) therefore consists entirely of maximum-weight edges of a cycle.
refutation_explanation: The claim asserts that no maximum-weight edge of any cycle in G can belong to the MST. In the witness graph, whichever MST one takes, both of its edges have weight equal to the maximum weight (1) on the cycle containing them, so the MST contains maximum-weight cycle edges - directly contradicting the claim. The correct cycle property requires the maximum-weight edge of the cycle to be UNIQUE (strictly heavier than all other cycle edges); the quoted claim drops that uniqueness hypothesis, and with weight ties it is false. The violation is robust to the ambiguity of 'the MST': every MST of the witness graph, not merely some MST, contains a cycle-maximum edge.
search_space: All simple connected undirected graphs on n in {3,4} labeled vertices containing at least one cycle (every edge subset of the complete graph with >= n edges, filtered for connectivity), with every assignment of integer weights from {1,2} to the edges. For each graph: all spanning trees enumerated by brute force over (n-1)-edge subsets, exact minimum weight and full MST set computed with integer arithmetic, all simple cycles enumerated as connected edge subsets with all degrees equal to 2. Deterministic lexicographic iteration order; a witness is reported only if EVERY MST of the graph contains a maximum-weight edge of some cycle. The first witness in this order is the all-weight-1 triangle on 3 vertices.
